   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?

   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?

   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?

   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Progressive fits Gardner's Rule Breaker traits only partly: it is the top challenger in a very old industry, has a strong brand (Flo) and a top-ranked culture, but US auto insurance is not an emerging market and the stock has lagged over the past year (about -3.5%). It is closer to a 'Rule Maker' compounder than a Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: Progressive matches many Buffett tenets: a simple business with an underwriting edge, low-cost float (2025 combined ratio 87.4%), 34.4% trailing return on equity and candid management. Against that, auto insurance is a commodity with weak switching costs, and Buffett's own GEICO is its closest rival, so the moat rests on execution, not structure.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire Progressive's long record of disciplined underwriting, its focus on a 96 combined ratio and its incentive design that ties pay to growth and profit targets. The main 'invert' risks are a price war in a commodity product, regulation of profits, and long-run disruption from safer, self-driving cars.
summaries.lynch: Under Lynch's labels Progressive is a stalwart-turned-fast-grower whose revenue compounded about 21% a year from 2022 to 2025, at about 11 times trailing earnings. But EPS is expected to fall in 2027 as rate cuts and competition squeeze margins, so the PEG is unattractive and the story now hinges on policy growth outlasting the soft market.
summaries.fisher: Progressive scores well on Fisher's points on salesmanship (direct plus 40,000+ agencies), cost analysis and management depth, and it keeps developing products such as Snapshot, Progressive Home and commercial lines. It does not spend on R&D in the usual sense, and growth is cyclical rather than a long string of new products.
summaries.graham: Progressive passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and EPS growth tests ($2.15 in 2015 to $19.23 in 2025), and at about 11 times trailing earnings its P/E is under 15. It fails his dividend test (no annual dividend for 2008) and P/E times P/B (about 11 x 3.7 = about 40) is well above 22.5.
summaries.thiel: Progressive is a strong operator in a crowded market rather than a Thiel-style monopoly: its pricing edge is meaningful but not ten times better than rivals, and it did not start from a small niche it dominated. It does have excellent distribution and a durable position.
summaries.gerstner: Progressive is a high-quality, very profitable compounder with a 12.6% free-cash-flow yield and a forward P/E around 13.7, which suits Gerstner's focus on efficiency and fair price. It is not tied to the AI/compute platform shift he favours, and slowing growth (premiums +4% in Q3 2026) argues against high conviction.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller looks for accelerating earnings and rising estimates; Progressive shows the opposite now, with 2027 EPS forecast to fall about 11% and premium growth slowing as the auto insurance cycle softens. Higher rates help its investment income, but the setup is late-cycle rather than inflecting up.
summaries.smith: Progressive meets Terry Smith's quality tests: high returns on capital (ROE about 33%), strong cash generation, low leverage and a growing market share. Its weaknesses are cyclical margins rather than steady ones and no gross margin in his sense, and it is reasonably priced at about 11 times trailing earnings.
summaries.greenblatt: On Magic Formula measures Progressive looks attractive: EV/EBIT of about 9 (an earnings yield near 11%) and a return on capital in the high 20s. As an insurer it is usually excluded from Greenblatt's screen, so the result should be read with care.
summaries.akre: Progressive fits Akre's stool reasonably well: an extraordinary business (No. 2 US auto insurer with a cost and pricing edge), skilled and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest float and capital as it grows. The reinvestment leg is limited by cyclicality and by large variable dividends paid out when capital is surplus.
summaries.pabrai: Progressive is a sound, low-risk business but not a Dhandho bet: it is a widely followed large cap without a temporary distress that creates a 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' price. Its strength lowers the chance of permanent loss, but the upside is not asymmetric.
summaries.wood: Progressive is not a disruptive-innovation stock in ARK's sense: it pioneered usage-based auto insurance, but it is not a leader in AI, robotics or the other platforms ARK tracks, and autonomous driving is more of a long-term threat to it.
summaries.ackman: Progressive matches several of Ackman's criteria: simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative, dominant in a large market and conservatively financed. Earnings are more cyclical than he prefers and there is no catalyst or mispricing to fix, so it would be a quality holding rather than an activist idea.
summaries.sleep: Progressive comes close to Nick Sleep's 'scale economies shared' model: it uses its size and data to price lower and win share, gaining from 13.3% to 18.6% of US auto in five years. The open question is whether that sharing can keep going in a soft market without hurting returns.
summaries.valentine: Progressive is not a Sequoia-style venture opportunity: it serves a huge market, but it is a mature insurer, not a young company riding a new technology wave.
summaries.nash: Progressive scores well on Nash's quality and valuation tests (about 80 on the 13 categories, strong DCF value, high free cash flow) but fails several hard filters: revenue growth below 10% in 2026, an operating margin below 20%, and no secular trend. It is a quality insurer rather than the kind of trend-driven growth stock Nash's process targets.

momentum.evidence: The share price ($218.49 on Oct 16, 2026) was down about 3.5% over the past 52 weeks, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Tricia Griffith (Fortune Businessperson of the Year 2018) leads a deep management bench, and institutions own about 89% of the shares.

g6.evidence: Analysts mostly rate it Hold (24 analysts, average target about $232); the main worry is slowing growth, not an overvalued stock.

simple.evidence: It sells car, home and business insurance and invests the premiums, an easy model to understand.

b2.evidence: It has stayed profitable every year since 2015 and grew revenue from $20.9B in 2015 to $87.7B in 2025.

integrity.evidence: Progressive publishes unusually detailed monthly results, pays out surplus capital through variable dividends ($13.50 annual dividend declared Dec 2025) and ties bonuses to growth and combined-ratio targets.

b6.evidence: It grows mainly organically and kept a 96 combined-ratio discipline rather than chasing large acquisitions, including during the 2022-2023 period when it cut back growth to restore margins.

roic.evidence: Trailing return on equity was 34.4% at Sept 30, 2026 with debt only 19.6% of total capital.

fcf.evidence: 2025 operating cash flow was $17.55B against net income of $11.31B, with capital spending of only $348M.

b10.evidence: Book value per share reached $59.51 in Sept 2026 and the market value is about $127B, far above the earnings it retained over the past decade, while also paying large dividends.

safety.evidence: At about 11 times trailing earnings and a 12.6% free-cash-flow yield the price looks undemanding, but insurer cash flow includes float, and EPS is expected to fall in 2027.

fairprice.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 11 and forward P/E of about 13.7 is reasonable for a business earning a 30%+ return on equity.

mu5.evidence: Low leverage and a short-duration portfolio (3.6 years) make collapse unlikely, but a price war, mispriced claims inflation or regulatory caps on profit could hurt it.

reinvest.evidence: Strong premium growth needs capital and earns high returns, but in soft markets it returns surplus capital through dividends instead of reinvesting.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart/fast grower in auto insurance whose story is simple: win share by pricing better than rivals.

ly3.evidence: With 2027 EPS forecast to fall about 11%, earnings growth is below the P/E of about 11.

runway.evidence: Progressive can keep gaining share in auto, grow Progressive Home and commercial lines, but it is already No. 2 with 18.6% of a mature US market.

ly7.evidence: Diluted shares fell to 582.2M in Q3 2026 from 588.2M a year earlier through buybacks, but insiders own only about 0.27% and mainly receive stock awards.

ly8.evidence: It is a widely covered S&P 500 large cap followed by 24 analysts.

fi2.evidence: It keeps adding products such as Snapshot, Progressive Home, bundling and small-business commercial lines.

fi3.evidence: Its investments in pricing models, telematics and technology show up in share gains (13.3% to 18.6% of US auto, 2020-2025), though it does not report R&D.

fi4.evidence: It sells directly online and by phone and through more than 40,000 independent agencies, backed by one of the industry's largest ad budgets.

longterm.evidence: Progressive grows as fast as it can at a 96 combined ratio and keeps spending on advertising in good years, a long-term rather than short-term focus.

gr1.evidence: Market value about $127B and 2025 revenue of $87.7B.

ni10.evidence: Net income was positive every year from 2016 ($1.06B) through 2025 ($11.31B), including $721.5M in 2022.

gr4.evidence: Progressive declared no annual dividend for 2008 after a loss year, so it has no 20-year unbroken record.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $2.15 in 2015 to $19.23 in 2025.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 11, but against average earnings of the volatile last few years ($1.18 in 2022, $6.58 in 2023) the multiple is higher.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 11 times P/B of about 3.7 gives about 40, above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its pricing models and telematics are better but not ten times better than State Farm's, GEICO's or Allstate's.

timing.evidence: Strong capital and record margins in 2025 let it grow share, but the auto insurance cycle is softening in 2026 as rates fall.

th3.evidence: It started as a niche non-standard auto insurer in 1937 and grew over decades rather than dominating a small market first.

team.evidence: Long-tenured management led by Tricia Griffith, CEO since 2016 and with the company since 1988.

th5.evidence: It has one of the best distribution engines in insurance: direct digital sales plus more than 40,000 independent agencies.

durable.evidence: Its position in US auto should hold for a decade, but self-driving cars and carmaker-embedded insurance could shrink the market over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Selling auto insurance is a well-understood opportunity contested by many rivals.

trend.evidence: It is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift such as AI or cloud; autonomous vehicles are more threat than opportunity.

dr1.evidence: 2026 EPS is expected to be roughly flat and 2027 EPS to fall about 11% as rates come down.

dr2.evidence: Policies in force grew 6% to 40.5M by Sept 2026, but falling average premiums and rising competition may weigh on margins.

dr4.evidence: Higher interest rates raise its investment income, but rate and economic swings also move bond values and claim costs.

dr6.evidence: Continued policy growth and buybacks could help, but no clear catalyst is in sight beyond the insurance cycle.

dr7.evidence: Slowing premium growth and expected EPS decline argue against a large concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Insurers do not report gross margin; its 2025 pretax margin was 16.2%.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT of about 9 means operating profit is about 11% of enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: There is no setback; results are near record highs, with the cycle now softening.

pa4.evidence: Low debt (19.6% of capital), a 3.6-year bond duration and strong underwriting make permanent loss unlikely.

wo1.evidence: It is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: Insurance costs (claims) rise with car repair and medical inflation, not falling with volume.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: US auto insurance will not grow many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results depend on interest rates, car-part prices, tariffs, weather and regulation.

ns1.evidence: It uses scale and data to price lower, cutting rates in 2026 to win share while staying profitable.

ns4.evidence: It has been gaining share steadily, but autonomous driving creates long-term uncertainty.
